segments.text: Your first case is an old one. The senior investigator hands you a closed file from nineteen fifty-eight to nineteen sixty-one, and asks you to read it the way people at the time had to: one dated entry at a time.

In nineteen fifty-eight, a new sleeping drug called thalidomide went on sale in Britain. People thought it was safe because it was not a barbiturate. At this point, nothing in the file connects it with pregnancy.

Three years later, at a meeting of gynaecologists, doctors reported many babies born with malformations of a kind that had been rare before. Look at the bars. In the last year, nineteen sixty-one, the column jumps. A rare event that suddenly becomes common is what makes a cluster stand out. Now watch the switch. If this defect had always been common, the same births blend into the background, and nobody would have a reason to report them. Switch it back to rare, and the jump stands out again. Now it is your turn: flip the switch yourself, and compare the two pictures.
segments.hint: Flip the switch to always common, and back.

segments.text: In the same year, someone suggested that thalidomide might be the cause. That is a suspicion, not a finding. So far it rests only on doctors noticing the drug in some mothers' histories. The senior investigator's advice is this: before you write a cause next to a cluster, decide what you would need to know to prove it. Keep that list, because you will use it in every case in this course.

Descriptive epidemiology counts cases by time, place and person. The first thing that count tells you is the size of the problem. In nineteen sixty-one the size was clear: doctors were seeing far more malformed births than before.

Next, when you look at where and when the cases fall, you start to find clues. In this file the clue was a new sleeping drug, thalidomide, which had been on sale in Britain since nineteen fifty-eight.

Put the size and the clue together, and you get a supposition: thalidomide might be the cause. That supposition is a hypothesis, a guess based on what was observed, which a study can accept or reject. The doctors in nineteen sixty-one reached it informally. A descriptive study ends where a hypothesis begins, and an analytical study starts there and tests it. So everything that follows depends on how well the hypothesis is written.

The file now has a suspect, but a suspect is not yet a claim that a study can check. On the screen are four claims about smoking, the same example your textbook uses. Some of them sound scientific, but they still give a study nothing to measure. So, which of these claims could a study actually test? Make your prediction.

Many people choose "cigarette smoking causes lung cancer". Your textbook uses that very claim as its example of an incomplete hypothesis. It names a cause and a disease, but it does not say who, how much, or for how long, so no result could ever count against it. A claim that a study can test has five parts. First, the population: the people the claim is about. Then the cause, the exact exposure. Then the outcome, the disease we expect. Then the dose-response: how much exposure leads to how much disease. And last, the time-response: how long it takes from exposure to disease.

The bare claim already has two of these parts, the cause and the outcome. Each part you add puts a new line on the list of data beside the claim. If the claim says thirty to forty cigarettes a day, you must measure cigarettes per day. If it says after twenty years, you must measure years of smoking. Now tap the other three parts to add them, and watch the list grow.
segments.hint: Tap the three missing parts to add them.

segments.text: Now watch what happens when a part comes back out. Take out the time-response, and years of smoking leaves the list. You can no longer tell a twenty-year effect from a two-year one. Whatever you leave out of the claim is a measurement you will never make. Let us put it back. Now take any part out yourself, and see its line go.
segments.hint: Tap a part to take it out of the claim.

segments.text: A colleague has drafted a claim for a study in one district. It says: among men aged forty to sixty, smoking more than ten bidis a day causes oral cancer in five per cent of them. Which of the five parts of a testable hypothesis is missing?

Suppose the full claim lost its dose, and now read: smoking causes lung cancer in ten per cent of smokers after twenty years. Compared with the full claim, which measurement would the study no longer have to make?

In an analytical study we look at people one at a time, but the conclusion is about the whole population they came from. There are two observational ways to run such a study, case-control and cohort, and they start from opposite ends. The dots on the screen are people. They are there only to show the order of events.

A cohort study starts with people who do not have the disease, grouped by whether they were exposed, and follows them forward in time to see who falls ill. A case-control study works the other way. It starts with people who already have the disease, called cases, and people who do not, called controls, and then looks back to find out what they were exposed to.

Time always runs one way, from exposure to disease. In a cohort study the questions run the same way, from cause to effect, so the two arrows agree. Here is the cohort once more, and then the case-control study. Its inquiry arrow turns round, because the questions run against time, from effect back to cause. Try it yourself: choose a design, and drag the time handle all the way.
segments.hint: Choose a design, then drag the time handle all the way.

segments.text: Both designs ask the same two questions: are an exposure and a disease associated, and if they are, how strongly? They differ in where they start, and that difference decides what each design can measure. We come back to this in lessons three and five.
Here are some short descriptions of studies. Sort each one into the design it belongs to, cohort or case-control.
Let us go back to the nineteen sixty-one file. Investigators found forty-six mothers whose babies were born with malformations, and asked them which drugs they had taken early in pregnancy.
Forty-one of those forty-six mothers had taken thalidomide.
Your textbook also reports a second group: three hundred mothers of normal babies. None of them had taken the drug.
The table puts the two groups side by side. Almost all the mothers of affected babies had taken thalidomide, while not one of the three hundred mothers of normal babies had.

Notice which way this study looked. It started from the effect, the affected babies, and looked back for the cause. On the time line under the mothers, its inquiry arrow points against time, so this is a case-control design. Later, laboratory experiments confirmed that thalidomide damages the developing baby in the womb.

But check the file before you trust it. The forty-one of forty-six comes from Widukind Lenz's enquiry in Hamburg in nineteen sixty-two, and accounts of that enquiry describe no formal control group. The three hundred control mothers are your textbook's figure, and the accounts checked for this course do not mention them. A separate German study in nineteen sixty-two, by Weicker and colleagues, did use controls: thirty-four of fifty mothers of affected babies had taken the drug, against two of ninety control mothers.
The sources for both studies are listed on the screen.

Now imagine the file held only the first column. You would still have forty-one of forty-six, but you could not say whether that is high, or simply how common the drug was among all pregnant women at the time. Now bring the controls back yourself, and see what the comparison adds.
segments.hint: Show the controls, and compare the two columns.

segments.text: Suppose that in nineteen sixty-one, investigators had instead enrolled three hundred pregnant women who had taken thalidomide and three hundred who had not, and then waited to see which babies were born with malformations. These numbers are only for illustration. Which design is this, and which way does its inquiry run?

Now a live case. This one is made up for the course: the plant, the city and every number are invented. A hospital in an Indian city has diagnosed twenty men with a rare liver tumour over a few years. All twenty worked at the same plastics plant, and several of them cleaned the large tanks where the plastic is made. The hospital has asked for an investigation. The senior investigator's advice: write the claim you would test before you collect anything.

The board offers two wordings for each of the five parts. For the population, the plant's employment records can confirm men who worked at the plant, so that wording goes in, and its record joins the list of data under the claim. Now pick a wording for each of the other four parts. Each time, choose the wording that a record at the plant or the hospital could actually confirm.
segments.hint: Choose a wording for each of the other four parts.

segments.text: Now watch the vague wordings. If you choose exposure to chemicals as the cause, that line says it cannot be measured. If you choose eventually as the time, the same thing happens, because no record can tell eventually from never. A precise claim would say: among men who worked at the plant, at least five years of tank cleaning causes this tumour, with more years giving more risk, appearing ten or more years after first exposure.

This is the same invented case. The claim is: among men who worked at the plant, at least five years of tank cleaning causes this liver tumour, with more years giving more risk, appearing ten or more years after first exposure. Which record must the investigation collect for each man?

These numbers are illustrative too. The plant's records come back: fourteen of the twenty men with the tumour had cleaned the tanks. That is seventy per cent, and it is tempting to write case solved on the file.

Put that count in a table and the gap shows at once. The cases fill one column, but the column for a comparison group is empty, so there is nothing to set the fourteen against. As the senior investigator notes, fourteen of any twenty men at that plant might have cleaned the tanks.

If most of the workers did that job, you would see seventy per cent even if cleaning were harmless. So you now have a precise claim and one striking count, but nothing beside the count to compare it with. That leaves one question for the next file: whom do you compare the twenty cases with?

Suppose the investigators find that among men of the same ages at the plant who do not have the tumour, fourteen of every twenty had also cleaned the tanks. What would the cases' fourteen of twenty then tell you about tank cleaning?
